# Discussion

The multi‑environment evaluation of NLL × oat mixed cropping demonstrated that total NLL grain yield was maintained across five European locations, while several indicators showed an improved temporal and spatial grain-yield stability relative to the component pure stands. The productivity indices clarify why total yield was preserved despite the strong oat dilution. The LER did not differ significantly from unity, a result attributed to the high yield and therefore high LER variability across the years, resulting in no statistical differences. Additionally, non-elevated LERs of mixed crops strongly focussed on one component (i.e. NLLs) goes in line with former metaanalytical on replacement designs [@zustovi2024], evidencing the LER remaining non-elevated. In contrast, the elevated CPR highlighted interactive effects: the CPRs of the oat varieties were strongly elevated above unity and the CPR of the NLL varieties remained close to unity, yielding a high total CPR across all mixtures. Hence, in the mixture the cereal captured otherwise unused resources without suppressing the legume, supporting theoretical work that niche complementarity rather than simple compensation underlies mixture advantages [@demie2022]. Presumably, this effect is particularly pronounced for the oat crop due to their low sowing proportion, which increases each oat plant's access to resources. And conversely, the niche complementarity benefits the NLL in mixture to a lesser extent, since they were sown at 90% of the pure stand's original density [@jensen1996; @hauggaard-nielsen2001]. Across all varieties, the LER was consistetly observed to remain at it's reference level of one, while the oat and total CPR values were consistently elevated above one, indicating a system-level (global) advantage of mixed cropping. This pattern of maintained LER- and elevated CPR_oat and total CPR-values across all varieties investigated highlights a global mixed-cropping effect of said metrics, which is agnostic to variety-pairing. This reinforces the evidence that the overall mixed-cropping effect outweighs cultivar-specific effects, as reported for barley-pea mixtures and for maize in maize-cowpea mixtures [@hauggaard-nielsen2001; @watiki1993].

Using either fertilized or unfertilized oat monocultures as the reference for LER led to the same conclusion: LER did not differ significantly between baselines. This insensitivity likely reflects substantial spatiotemporal variance in yield across all environment-years and the low sowing proportion of oat in the mixtures, which diminishes the weight of the oat component in the summed LER, thus limiting statistical power. In contrast, both total CPR and oat‑specific CPR were higher when mixtures were benchmarked against unfertilized oat stands, revealing a fertilizer‑mediated gain in the performance of pure oat stands. Because CPR explicitly scales yields by the sown proportion of each species, it provides a proportion‑corrected measure and is therefore more sensitive than LER to management effects under imbalanced mixtures. These findings are consistent with the prior report of @baxevanos2020 that using unfertilized monocultures as references can yield larger estimates of intercropping advantage than using fertilized references.

While the static metric (CV) did not detect significant differences in grain‑yield stability, the two dynamic approaches, the Finlay-Wilkinson slope ($b_{1}$) and WAAS, revealed clear contrasts among treatments. In pure stands, fertilized oat Lion combined an above‑average responsiveness to environments (slope $b_{1} > 1$) with low dispersion around the regression, indicating a predictable response in both favorable and unfavorable conditions. Fertilization enhanced the stability of oat monocultures: in the present study, fertilized Lion and Troll showed significantly higher grain-yield stability (smaller WAAS) than their unfertilized counterparts, consistent with the findings of @silva2016. Most mixted stands exhibited elevated responsiveness to the environmental conditions ($b_{1} > 1$), while the most stable mixed treatments exhibited $b_{1} \approx 1$, coupled to low sensitivities to the environmental conditions WAAS. Such stability in cereal–pulse mixtures is commonly attributed to differential species responses and complementarity that buffer environmental variation and reduce $G \times E$ interaction, resulting in more stable yields amongst selected combinations [@raseduzzaman2017].

The increased dynamic grain-yield stability observed for mixed cropping in this study extends the findings of @weih2021 by showing that under a pulse-focussed replacement design (NLL × oat), mixture stability did not only match, but surpassed the pure‑crop benchmarks on dynamic grain-yield stability. This pattern re-affirms the findings by @raseduzzaman2017, that replacement-designed mixed crops of cereals and pulses elevate the grain-yield stability across environments. Notably, the most stable mixtures, namely Bison × Probor and Troll × Jowisz, emerged even though neither corresponding sole crop ranked among the most stable, underscoring that stability must be assessed at the mixture level rather than inferred from component monocultures. By quantifying stability with complementary dynamic metrics (Finlay–Wilkinson slope, $b_{1}$, and WAAS), the results of this study show that the stability advantage of mixtures is not confined to balanced designs; it also holds under replacement designs that emphasize the NLL component.

# Conclusion

This study focusses on the grain-yield performance and stability of pulse-cereal mixed cropping with regards to both pure stands and in mixtures. Further aspects of mixed cropping, such as economic viability, sowing methods, plant protection, threshing and processing and quality of harvested seeds need to be addressed as well. The patterns observed in the present study demonstrate that the right variety mixtures improve grain-yield stability of both the NLL and oat while maintaining the crop performance and land use, opening opportunities for tailoring mixtures to agri-environmental risk profiles. Moreover, the robust yield-stability advantage of mixtures across environment-years, which differed six‑fold in seasonal precipitation, suggests that mixed cropping can effectively hedge against increasing climate variability, aligning with policy aims to broaden on‑farm plant protein production. Hence, strategic variety pairing within mixed cropping emerges as an expedient lever to combine high crop yield and maintain land use performance while improving the production's resilience. These findings strengthen the evidence base for incorporating cereals into pulse-centric cropping strategies to enhance resilience under climate uncertainty and mitigate the pulses' yield instability.

Formula 1 - Eberhard-Russell regression for plot-level data
$$
Y_{ij} = \mu_i + b_1i\, I_j + \delta_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij} \tag{1}
$$

Where:

$Y_{ij}$ is the observed yield of the $i^{th}$ treatment in the $j^{th}$ environment,

$\mu_i$ is the mean yield of the $i^{th}$ treatment across all environments,
  
$b_{1i}$ is the Finlay–Wilkinson regression coefficient representing treatment $i$’s responsiveness to the environments,

$I_j$ is the environmental index, calculated as the mean yield of environment $j$ minus the grand mean across environments,

$\delta_{ij}$​ is the deviation from the linear response in environment $j$ used to compute the deviation variance $S^2_{di}$, and

$\varepsilon_{ij}$ is the residual term.

Formula 2 - Eberhart–Russell deviation variance

$$
S^2_{di} = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{E} \delta_{ij}^{\,2}}{E - 2} \tag{2}
$$

Where:

$\delta_{ij} = Y_{ij} - (\mu_i + b_{1i}I_j)$ are the deviations from the regression line and

$E$ are the number of environments.

Table S2: Statistical models deployed to analyse the data. The characteristics explain the details of the model. Each response variable (attribute) in the present study was analysed with one or more of the models listed in the table. To analyse the effect of canopy height difference onto the narrow-leaved lupin proportion and the total yield, model M3 was adapted replacing the predictor treatment with canopy height difference.
:::
| Model    | Characteristics                                 |
|----------|-------------------------------------------------|
| M1       | This model answered if the response variable differed in mixtures and pure NLLs (or analogously oats) across all varieties. It performed an ANOVA using the NLL/oat-variety and the binary variable stand = mixed. This model considered each species separately. |
| M2       | M2 answered if the response variable differed in mixtures and pure NLLs or oats. Here, this was achieved by computing the linear contrasts of each pure NLL/oat variety with the mean of its respective mixtures. This model considered each species separately. |
| M3       | On the subset of only mixed plots, M3 performed a two-way (mixed) ANOVA with the factors oat variety and NLL variety (adjusting for location, year, and block). This model considered both species together. Further, M3 performed post-hoc comparisons of the treatments and locations. |
| M4       | M4 answered the question, if the estimated value of the treatments with mixed stands (e.g. the land equivalent ratio) was significantly different from an expected value (e.g. LER = 1) after a Bonferroni correction (with the respective 12 coefficients). |
